</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

If your harness appears here, read its reference file for special instructions:

- Codex: `references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `references/antigravity-tools.md`
- Hermes Agent: `references/hermes-tools.md`
- Muse: `references/muse-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>"
  }
}

commands.name: skillator:build-jarvis

Style words switch tiers: "use fable", "cheap", "opus only", "full ceremony". NOT for a non-feature one-line edit (typo, comment, rename, formatting), an unexplained bug, UI-only polish or critique (design-arwen, tui-tron) or design with no code.

commands.name: skillator:build-ultron
commands.description: (skillator) Use only when the user names "build-ultron" itself. A retired name, kept for one release so old prompts and docs still resolve; it points at build-jarvis. NOT for any feature request that does not say this name - those go to build-jarvis directly.

commands.name: skillator:build-vision

commands.name: skillator:chief-fury
commands.description: (skillator) Use when one session is handed a long-running goal to own across weeks and sessions - "you own getting X to v1", "be the DRI", "chief of staff", "I'm away for a month, keep it moving", "I won't remember and neither will you" - or when a decision on such a goal touches several seats and needs a board meeting. NOT for one feature (`build-jarvis`), a staged run alone (`relay-morpheus`), a session handoff (`handoff-cortana`) or the board itself (`tickets-zordon`).

commands.name: skillator:code-yoda
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "yoda", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "yagni", "do less", complains about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate or an unnecessary dependency, asks what can be deleted from a diff or a whole repo, or - before a release or handover - asks what was knowingly deferred, shortcut, "left for later" or "should be tracked" in the code (`ponytail:` markers). NOT for correctness or security review (`code-review`, `audit-sherlock`) and NOT for the board itself (`tickets-zordon`).

commands.name: skillator:deploy-merlin
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "prep the deployment", "set up deploy", "deployment wizard", "get this ready to ship to my server", "scaffold the deploy", or is about to stand up a new app on a Linux VPS with the standard single-VPS pattern (Docker Compose + nginx + GitHub Actions, one-push deploy, maintenance gate, TLS via Let's Encrypt). NOT for non-VPS / managed-PaaS deploys, or for the actual server administration.

commands.name: skillator:deploy-niyoj
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "niyoj", "set up niyoj deploy", "deploy without CI", "manual deploy", "no github actions deploy", "one-button deploy from my laptop", when converting a project off `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, or when a NiYoj deploy failed and needs diagnosing. The target is a single-VPS app (Docker Compose + nginx + maintenance gate + Let's Encrypt) deployed over SSH from the NiYoj desktop app, with no CI runner. NOT for CI-triggered deploys (use `deploy-merlin`) or managed-PaaS targets.

commands.name: skillator:design-arwen
commands.description: (skillator) Use for UI-only work on a UI/UX, native or web - redesign, improve or critique a page, screen, dashboard, form or design system; make it less generic, bolder, less AI-made; pick fonts/colors/layout/motion; fix hierarchy, spacing, contrast, a11y or UI performance; write UX copy and error states; one design language across native and web - or when this skill is named. NOT for a UI feature to build (build-jarvis runs this as its UI design step), backend or non-UI work.

commands.name: skillator:designui-galadriel
commands.description: (skillator) Use when an EXISTING UI-only mockup must become real and working - the user says their app is "just a UI", "not functional", "fake / hardcoded data", "no backend", "the buttons don't do anything", or asks to "make it real", "wire it up", "connect it to a backend/API/database". Ends at a confirmed plan; does not build. NOT for Figma-to-UI, design/UX/a11y review, styling bugs, debugging a feature that already works, a brand-new app with no mockup, or backend-only fixes.

commands.name: skillator:grayskull-power
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "dev mode", "activate the programming skills", "turn on the skillator workflow", "use our skills", "by the power of grayskull", "grayskull", "check screenshot", "set up for coding", or starts real development work in a repo with no skillator skill active. The single entry point that routes each request to the right skillator skill; it does not do the work itself. NOT for enabling/disabling skills on disk.

commands.name: skillator:handoff-cortana
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user asks to "hand off", "write a handoff", "create a handoff doc", "document where we are", "prepare for the next session/person", or wants a continuity/checkpoint summary of the current session — an in-depth, verified session-handoff document (a Markdown file) so a different person or AI can continue the work with zero loss of context, plan, or intent.

commands.name: skillator:holo-r2d2
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "Help me, Obi-Wan", "help me obiwan" or "help me obi wan kenobi" - alone, with a run (RUN-12) or a ticket (F39), even while a run is parked: it means "draw it". Also to show a run, its decisions, a plan or a design as a diagram, and when several owner decisions need answering - the decision wizard. NOT for answering or ruling decisions (`relay-morpheus`), NOT the ticket board (`tickets-zordon`).

commands.name: skillator:live-friday
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "let me see it", "show me while you work", "don't make me wait", "live preview", "run it while you build", "stream the build", or whenever a change is about to be made to a project that has a runnable surface — JS/web dev server, Rust, C++, Python, Go, Electron, mobile or a plain CLI. Armed as standard by grayskull-power. NOT for taking screenshots (screenshot-argus) and NOT a substitute for tests — it is exposure, not verification.

commands.name: skillator:merge-smith
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user wants to combine/consolidate several GitHub branches into one integration branch, merge a feature branch into a base (main/develop), or reconcile divergent branches that touched the same code — and wants conflicts handled intelligently rather than by hand. The merge direction (`<source>` INTO `<destination>`) is confirmed before anything is touched; the base branch is never touched directly and nothing is pushed without explicit approval. NOT for a single trivial fast-forward, or non-git tasks.

commands.name: skillator:mergeprep-oracle
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user wants to "prep a branch for merge", "clean up a branch before merging", "make sure only the real changes get merged", "strip stale/old parts", or is about to run merge-smith and wants the branch normalized first. Everything happens ON THE BRANCH ITSELF — never a side branch, never a history rewrite, never a force-push, never the base. NOT for the actual merge (use merge-smith) or for non-git tasks.

commands.name: skillator:relay-morpheus
commands.description: (skillator) Use when work runs in stages and the session may not survive to their end — a multi-stage plan, fan-out, a sleeping laptop, a dropping link, a usage limit. Also on "marathon", "May the Force be with you", "Use the Force on F35 F36", "work the board", "keep going", "I'll be back", "I'm back", "ask me everything at the end", "resume the run". NOT for a session handoff (`handoff-cortana`), the board (`tickets-zordon`) or drawing a run ("Help me, Obi-Wan" — `holo-r2d2`).

commands.name: skillator:remote-cerebro
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user wants to drive codex, cursor-agent, pi or gemini from a phone or another device: "remote control", "control pi remotely", "drive codex from my phone", "keep working away from the desk", "I'm leaving my desk", a Telegram bot for a coding agent, pairing a phone to a CLI, or turning approvals off so the phone needs fewer taps. NOT for Claude Code (use its own Remote Control) and NOT for dispatching other CLIs from this session.

commands.name: skillator:resume-cortana
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "execute the handoff", "run the handoff", "work through the handoffs", "pick up the pending tasks", "resume from the handoff doc(s)", "do the next tasks in the handout", "process docs/handoffs", or wants a repeatable pass — safe to re-run or /loop — that picks up where a handoff left off. The execution counterpart to handoff, which writes the doc. NOT for writing a handoff (use handoff), and not for arbitrary tasks that live outside a handoff document.

commands.name: skillator:rules-orko

commands.name: skillator:screenshot-argus
commands.description: (skillator) Use when the user says "screenshots", "check the screenshots", "I dropped new screenshots", "test screenshots", "look at the latest run", or gives a screenshot directory path — test screenshots dropped in a project's screenshot folder that need acting on and then clearing. NOT for taking screenshots (use a browser/app skill for that) and NOT for permanent design assets — everything in that folder is treated as disposable.

commands.name: skillator:skill-smith
commands.description: (skillator) Use when writing a new agent skill, editing an existing one, or diagnosing a skill agents don't load or don't follow - a SKILL.md, slash command, reference file, or always-on file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md). Also when the user says "write a skill", "make this a skill", "skillify this", "my skill isn't triggering", "the agent ignored the skill", "improve this skill", or asks why a rule keeps getting rationalized away. NOT for using a skill or installing one.

commands.name: skillator:spec-watson

Also on requests for spec-driven development, spec-kit, specify/plan/tasks artifacts, or a traceability matrix. NOT for requirements already carrying stable identifiers, and not for a one-off edit.

commands.name: skillator:tasks-sentinels

commands.name: skillator:teams-uhura

commands.name: skillator:tickets-zordon

commands.name: claude-mem:learn-codebase

commands.name: claude-mem:make-plan

commands.name: claude-mem:mem-search

commands.name: claude-mem:mode-creator

commands.name: claude-mem:screenpipe

commands.name: claude-mem:standup

commands.name: claude-mem:timeline-report

commands.name: claude-mem:weekly-digests

Use when asked for "weekly digests", "week-by-week story", "serial timeline", or "narrative chapters" of a project's history.

commands.name: claude-mem:what-the

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\Ikran\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--tools-Projects-skillator2\66a4199e-bee7-472b-9aaa-61fc26982c2a\scratchpad\f100\put\skills\build-jarvis

# build-jarvis — every feature, graded, designed, built

The one build skill. It **is** `PRACTICE.md` §§1-6 for a feature, design
included, so nothing runs in front of it — not `superpowers:brainstorming`, not
`writing-plans`, not a second `build-*`. You are the **orchestrator**: you grade,
dispatch, rule and keep the record. Design and code run in subagents, each with
an explicit model, because a skill cannot change the main session's model.

Read **`PRACTICE.md`** first — beside `PLATFORMS.md`, at the plugin root (`../`
in the `install.sh` layout, `../../` in a checkout or the plugin cache). It owns
classification, questions, the TASKS shape, self-review, test-first, evidence
and review. Everything below assumes it.

## Step 0 — GRADE, before anything is spent

0. **Not a build after all?** A request that only changes how an existing
   screen looks or reads - polish, redesign, critique, fonts/colours/spacing/
   contrast, "less generic", UX copy, an a11y pass, a frame that draws wrong -
   with no new behaviour, or one that names design-arwen / tui-tron, is handed
   straight to that skill: one line `ui-only -> design-arwen` (or `tui-tron`),
   load it, no grade line, no design file. This is the one Step 0 exit that
   prints no `grade:` line (the grade gate guards Write and Agent only; a Skill
   call is not gated, so the hand-off passes).
1. **Classify** spike / bounded / architectural (PRACTICE §1).
2. **Criticality.** The work is **critical** when it touches auth, money,
   concurrency, or a contract others depend on (a shared API, a file format, a
   schema). Say which word made it critical.
3. **Tier each seat** from this table — the same one as `practice/task-loop.md`
   § Model selection and `tickets-zordon`'s scout:

   | The work reads like | design | build | verify |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | One file, mechanical, the change is named | — | cheap | build |
   | 1-2 files, complete spec, nothing left to decide | — | cheap | build |
   | Several files, integration, or choices left open | deep | build | build |
   | Cause unknown, design judgement, architectural | deep | build | deep |
   | Critical (any row) | deep | build | **deep, held** |

   Critical's build seat is the **build** tier (`build=opus` on Claude Code,
   per `PLATFORMS.md`), never cheap.

   `—` = no design pass: the request or ticket *is* the spec, and you write it
   into the design file as its one task. **build is the floor** for every verify
   seat and for a build seat working from prose rather than named code.

   **ui** - `arwen` (web/native surface), `tron` (terminal UI), `none`; the
   field sits between ceremony and mode
   ([references/grade.md § The ui field](references/grade.md#the-ui-field)).
4. **Tier → model:** read `.skillator/tiers.local.md` (written by
   `grayskull-power`'s `tiers` arm step). Missing → the first slug in your
   host's column of `PLATFORMS.md` § Role tiers, and say `tiers: defaults`.
5. **Step down, never up on your own** — the one exception is Phase 2's
   third fix round, and only with its `Ruling:` line:
   - a tier whose model the file marks `down:` → that seat goes one tier lower;
   - usage ≥ 70 % of the 5-hour window (`watch-cortana`'s `usage-watch.* level`,
     the `5h=` field) → every **non-critical** seat one tier lower; `src=none`
     → no step-down, and say `usage unobservable`;
   - never below cheap, never a verify seat below build, and a **held** seat
     keeps the highest tier still available.
   Every downgrade is a line: `Ruling: <seat> <from>-><to> - <why> - <cost if wrong>`.
6. **User words win over the table** (unavailability still wins over them):
   "use fable" / "fable designs" → design and deep seats on fable · "opus only"
   / "all opus" → every seat opus · "cheap" / "on a budget" → every
   non-critical seat one tier lower · "top tier" / "best models" → every seat
   deep · a named model → that seat on it.
7. **Your first reply text after loading this skill is the grade line** —
   before the design-file Write, before any Agent call. No confirmation gate
   (step 8's mode question is the one Step 0 ask); the line is there so the
   user can overrule before the first token is spent:

   ```
   grade: bounded · critical no · design - · build cheap=sonnet · verify build=opus · ceremony lean · ui none · mode ask (single) · usage 5h 41%
   ```

   **Printed means reply text the user sees**, starting `grade:`, before the
   design file is written or anything is dispatched. A grade worked out in your
   thinking, a `Ruling: critical no` in the design file, or a summary at the
   end is not printed — the user cannot overrule a line they never saw.

   **The line is a required input.** It is the design file's first line and
   the first line of every Agent prompt (design, build, verify), verbatim. So
   whichever spend comes first — the design-file Write *or* a design agent —
   print the line as reply text, then paste the same line into that call.
8. **Mode — the grade line's `mode` field, settled before any spend.** How
   Phase 2 runs:

   | Mode | What runs | Fits |
   |---|---|---|
   | **single** | One build agent does every task in order; design and verify stay their own seats | `—` design seat, 1-3 tightly coupled tasks, tasks sharing files |
   | **per-task** | One fresh build agent per task (`tasks-sentinels`); same-file tasks never fan out | Several independent tasks — the usual pick when nothing else fits |
   | **workflow** | Phases 1-3 as one workflow script (`WORKFLOW.md`); no `Workflow` tool → the host's parallel subagents | 4+ independent tasks or a sweep — costs the most tokens |

   - `mode ask (<recommended>)` — the default. Right after the grade line, ask
     once: all three modes, your recommendation first (`AskUserQuestion`; no
     such tool → a numbered list). Then **end your turn** — no design-file
     Write, no Agent, until the user answers. Then reprint the line with
     `mode <m> (asked)`; that line is the one the design file and every
     Agent prompt carry.
   - `mode <m> (named)` — the user already named one ("single agent", "one
     agent per task", "use a workflow", "ultracode"). No question.
   - `mode <m> (ruled)` — the prompt or run says headless, chained or inside a
     relay. No question; log `Ruling: mode <m> - <why> - <cost if wrong>`.
     A bare feature request is not headless, whatever tools you lack.

   Recommend from the grade row and how coupled the work reads. **Never
   workflow without the user's opt-in**: unasked, the most you pick is per-task.

**Ceremony** is `full` when the work is architectural, has 4+ tasks, runs
inside a relay run, or is said to outlive this session ("keep going after",
"hand it over", "full ceremony"); otherwise `lean`. Full adds the session
record, the handoff checkpoint, the TRACE table and the rework loop —
**[references/ceremony.md](references/ceremony.md)**.

Grade detail, the tiers file, the unavailable-at-dispatch retry and worked
examples: **[references/grade.md](references/grade.md)**.

## Design questions — ruled or parked, never asked mid-build

- **Decidable** from the repo, the ticket, PRACTICE or a stated rule → rule it
  and write it into the design file's `## Decisions`:
  `Ruling: <what> - <why> - <cost if wrong>`.
- **Only the user can answer** (taste, a fact only they hold, a conflict nothing
  settles) → `relay-morpheus park`, and build everything that does not depend on
  it. A relay run in flight → park on its stage. A standalone build → open a
  one-stage run first so the park has a home (commands in
  [references/grade.md](references/grade.md#parking-from-a-standalone-build)).
- **The six stops** (destructive op, security-sensitive action, a side effect
  outside this worktree, the 7-day limit at 90 %, a scope breach, a failed
  repro) → ask now, alone.
- **Architectural** keeps PRACTICE §1's one approval gate after the design is
  written and reviewed — asked when the user is present, parked when the run is
  headless, chained or the user is away.
- "ask me as you go", "brainstorm with me", "let's design it together" →
  live questions instead, one at a time (PRACTICE §1); each answer still lands
  in `## Decisions`.

## Phase 1 — Design

Design seat `—` → write the design file yourself from the request. Otherwise
dispatch one design agent on the design seat's model with the request verbatim,
the repo context and `PRACTICE.md`; it writes the file and returns only its path
plus two lines:

```
grade: <the Step 0 line, verbatim - also already printed as reply text>
GOAL:         <the task in one line>
CHOSEN:       <the approach + why; architectural lists 2-3 APPROACHES first>
DESIGN:       <data model / contracts, key edge cases, out of scope>
CONSTRAINTS:  <what stays true across every task - exact values, names,
              formats; copied verbatim into every reviewer as
              [GLOBAL_CONSTRAINTS]>
TASKS:        <one block per task in PRACTICE §2 shape (Files, Interfaces,
              test-first steps with real code and commands), each tagged
              build=<tier> from the Step 0 table>
VERIFICATION: <the exact end-to-end command and its expected output>
## Decisions  <every Ruling: made so far; parked questions by Q-id>
```

Lean: `design-<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` in the scratchpad. Full:
`docs/sessions/session-<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md`, plus the REQUIREMENTS / TRACE
slots in [references/ceremony.md](references/ceremony.md).

This core design is architecture, interfaces and workflow - no UI craft; a UI
task block says only what the surface must do (states, data, keys), not how it
looks.

**UI design pass** (`ui` not `none`) — after the core file is written: one
agent on the design seat's model (a `—` seat: the build seat's) with this
prompt:

```
<grade line verbatim>
Load skillator:design-arwen (mode build for a new surface, improve for a change to one) and read the design file at <path> first. Design the UI for the TASKS that touch a surface, on top of the core design - never change DESIGN, CONSTRAINTS or the interfaces. Append a section `## UI design` (the signature, screens/states, hierarchy, platform notes, the a11y floor) and rewrite each UI task block's steps so an implementer builds that design (real code, test-first). Return the file path and the section's first line.
```

`ui tron`: the same prompt with `Load skillator:tui-tron`, and the section holds
the width matrix (the widths the app must draw at), the capture command per
width and the frame each must show; those captures go into VERIFICATION as the
render proof. Ops-board pane work: its `claude plugin test` frame assertions
are the render proof; a width matrix only for the standalone ops app.
`ui arwen+tron`: two passes, arwen first.

Then self-review once (PRACTICE §3), both sections, and fix inline. A
`ui tron` VERIFICATION without the captured frames is unmet (Phase 3). A
**spike** stops at Phase 1: the probe and a recommendation, nothing kept.

## Phase 2 — Build

The Step 0.8 mode decides the shape. **per-task**: one agent per task, each on
its own tagged tier; independent tasks fan out, same-file tasks do not.
**single**: one build agent takes every task block in order, on the highest
tagged tier, and reports per block. Either way a build agent gets fresh context,
the **design file path** and its task block(s) — never the design pasted, never
this session's history (PRACTICE §4; procedure `practice/task-loop.md`, prompt
text `practice/prompts.md`). Several F tickets are one pass, one task block per
ticket; a build agent implements its block(s) only — it never loads this skill,
regrades or runs its own verify. Review each block against its spec before the
next dispatch; a failed review goes to a fix agent. A third round may go one
tier up, and only with
`Ruling: <seat> <from>-><to> - reviews <1> and <2> failed: <why each failed> - <cost if wrong>`
citing both failed reviews; no Ruling, no step up.

**Mode workflow** (the user opted in) → run Phases 1-3 as one workflow script
(`WORKFLOW.md`): write the design file first, pass its path in `args`, and the
build stage reads each task's tier: `model: M[t.build]`.

## Phase 3 — Verify, review, relay

Run VERIFICATION through PRACTICE §5 — the command, now, in full, exit code
read — on the verify seat. Anything bigger than bounded, or critical, gets one
whole-diff review on the verify seat's tier (PRACTICE §6,
`code-review:code-review`). Failures go back through Phase 2's fix loop. Then
relay: the grade line again as the report's first line, what was built
(files), the verification evidence, every Ruling, every parked Q-id.

## Rules

- **Grade before spending.** No design file, no dispatch, before the grade
  line is printed as reply text.
- **A budget is a step-down, never a merge.** A spend cap (`--max-budget-usd`,
  "on a budget", a cost ceiling) means "cheap" — every non-critical seat one
  tier lower, said in a `Ruling:`. It never reaches critical work: critical
  keeps its deep design seat (a dispatched design agent) and its deep, held
  verify. It never folds the seats into this session:
  a subagent costs no more than the same work done here, and the orchestrator
  that builds has nobody to verify it.

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "I graded it — it's in my reasoning / the design file's Rulings." | Not printed. The line exists so the user can overrule it before spend; invisible, it overrules nothing. |
| "Small and obvious; the grade line is ceremony." | It is one line. Size does not waive it; `design -` already says it was small. |
| "The budget won't cover subagents, so I'll design, build and verify here." | Same tokens, minus the second pair of eyes. Step seats down; keep them separate. |
| "Critical work — safer if I do it all myself." | Critical makes verify **deep, held**: a different seat, not this one. |
| "The cap reads as cheap, so the critical design seat drops to build." | The step-down is for non-critical seats only. Critical design stays deep and dispatched. |

**Red flag:** about to Write the design file, or call Agent — a design agent
included — with no `grade:` line in your reply text yet, or with `mode ask`
still unanswered: stop and print or ask first. Critical work is no exception;
it is where the overrule matters most.
- **Never an unnamed model.** An omitted model inherits the session's.
- **The design file is the handover.** Pass it by path; the orchestrator does
  not design or code, bar writing a `—`-seat design file and the record.
- **Autonomous, honest.** A phase that fails or an agent that returns nothing is
  said plainly; nothing continues on a missing piece.
- **Handoff before context loss.** About to `/compact` or `/clear` → run
  `handoff-cortana` first.

## Other hosts

`PLATFORMS.md` turns tiers into slugs and dispatch into the host's delegate
mechanism; no delegation → run the seats sequentially in one session, each
phase's output written to disk before the model switch. Per-host notes, the
seat table and the Opus-version limit: [references/platforms.md](references/platforms.md).
The `UserPromptSubmit` route hook that puts a feature prompt here on Claude
Code: [references/route-hook.md](references/route-hook.md).

# shelf

A book catalogue CLI, in memory.

    python -m shelf add "Dune" "Frank Herbert"
    python -m shelf find Dune
    python -m shelf report

Board: TICKETS.md. Tests: `python -m pytest`.

==> conftest.py <==

==> shelf/__init__.py <==

==> shelf/__main__.py <==
import sys

from shelf.cli import main

sys.exit(main())

==> shelf/books.py <==
"""The catalogue, in memory."""
_BOOKS = []


def add(title, author):
    book = {"title": title, "author": author}
    _BOOKS.append(book)
    return book


def find(query):
    return [b for b in _BOOKS if query in b["title"]]


def all_books():
    return list(_BOOKS)


def clear():
    _BOOKS.clear()

==> shelf/cli.py <==
import argparse

from shelf import books, report


def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="shelf")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    a = sub.add_parser("add")
    a.add_argument("title")
    a.add_argument("author")
    f = sub.add_parser("find")
    f.add_argument("query")
    sub.add_parser("report")
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    if args.cmd == "add":
        books.add(args.title, args.author)
    elif args.cmd == "find":
        for b in books.find(args.query):
            print("%s - %s" % (b["title"], b["author"]))
    else:
        print(report.summary())
    return 0

==> shelf/report.py <==
"""One-line summary of the catalogue."""
from shelf import books


def summary():
    return "%d books" % len(books.all_books())

==> tests/test_books.py <==
from shelf import books, report


def setup_function():
    books.clear()


def test_add_then_find():
    books.add("Dune", "Frank Herbert")
    assert books.find("Dune") == [{"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert"}]


def test_report_counts_books():
    books.add("Dune", "Frank Herbert")
    books.add("Emma", "Jane Austen")
    assert report.summary() == "2 books"


def test_report_on_empty_shelf():
    assert report.summary() == "0 books"

1	# PRACTICE.md — skillator's process canon
2	
3	The craft every skillator skill works to. It is **merged in, not borrowed**: the
4	substance of the superpowers process skills lives here, in skillator's own words,
5	so no skillator skill has to defer to an external plugin at runtime or chain one
6	in front of itself.
7	
8	| Section | Merged from |
9	|---|---|
10	| §1 Classify · question · scope · show it | `superpowers:brainstorming` (its visual companion routed to `design-arwen`'s artboard gate) |
11	| §2 Tasks are a plan | `superpowers:writing-plans`, `executing-plans` |
12	| §3 Self-review the design | `writing-plans` + `brainstorming` spec review |
13	| §4 Building | `skillator:tasks-sentinels`, `test-driven-development`, `subagent-driven-development`, `dispatching-parallel-agents` |
14	| §5 Claiming it works | `verification-before-completion` |
15	| §6 Reviewing, and taking review | `requesting-code-review`, `receiving-code-review` |
16	| §7 Debugging | `systematic-debugging` |
17	| §8 Branch lifecycle | `using-git-worktrees`, `finishing-a-development-branch` |
18	
19	The thirteenth, `writing-skills`, is merged into `skillator:skill-smith` rather
20	than here — it is a surface with its own workflow, not a rule the other skills
21	obey.
22	
23	This file is the **laws** — read in full by `grayskull-power` (§0) and
24	`build-jarvis` (before its Step 0 grade), once per session. The
25	mechanics sit in `practice/`, read on demand when a section sends you there:
26	
27	| File | Load when |
28	|---|---|
29	| [`practice/prompts.md`](practice/prompts.md) | Dispatching any subagent — the five templates, verbatim |
30	| [`practice/task-loop.md`](practice/task-loop.md) | Driving a design's tasks to done — setup, seat tiers, fix rounds, final review |
31	| [`practice/scripts/taskwork.sh`](practice/scripts/taskwork.sh) (`.ps1`) | Generating a task brief or a review package as a file, so a diff never lands in the controller's context. It lives beside these docs — `<practice>/scripts/`, never in the user's project — so resolve its absolute path first: [`practice/task-loop.md` § Where taskwork.sh lives](practice/task-loop.md#where-taskworksh-lives) |
32	| [`practice/tdd.md`](practice/tdd.md) | Writing or changing tests — the cycle, what makes a test honest, the canonical excuse table (§4 below carries nine of its eleven rows verbatim; go there for all of them) |
33	| [`practice/debugging.md`](practice/debugging.md) | §7 says *trace it* — backward tracing, defense in depth, flaky tests, test pollution |
34	
35	`PLATFORMS.md` owns host mechanics and `WORKFLOW.md` owns fan-out scripts; this
36	file owns *how the work is done*. It is craft, not a phase list — the phases live
37	in each SKILL.md.
38	
39	---
40	
41	## 1. Classify before you design (`superpowers:brainstorming`)
42	
43	Say the classification out loud in the first reply so the user can override it.
44	It sets how much of everything below applies.
45	
46	| Path | What it is | Ceremony |
47	|---|---|---|
48	| **Spike** | A feasibility question. Output is an answer, not code you keep. | 2-3 sentences of intent, a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design file. Anything built is labelled throwaway. |
49	| **Bounded** | A scoped change to a flow that **already exists in this repo** to read. | Clarifying questions, a short design in chat, then build. Design file optional — write it if the build will span a context checkpoint. |
50	| **Architectural** | New project, new subsystem, or a change that restructures how components fit or alters an interface others depend on. | The full phase list: 2-3 approaches, sectioned design, design file, self-review, **one approval gate**, then build. |
51	
52	**Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity.** Knowing the kind of app is
53	not enough — if there is no existing flow to change, it is architectural.
54	
55	In doubt between two, take the heavier one. The ratchet is one-way: hidden
56	complexity found mid-build upgrades the path — stop, say so, step up. Nothing
57	downgrades mid-task.
58	
59	**Oversized requests:** if the ask spans several independent subsystems, say so
60	before spending questions on details. Decompose into sub-projects, name the
61	order, and run the first one through the full cycle. Each sub-project gets its
62	own design file.
63	
64	### The one approval gate
65	
66	`superpowers:brainstorming` gates *every* path on explicit user approval before
67	implementation. This skill keeps autonomy for **spike** and **bounded** — that is
68	the deliberate difference, and it is why the classification is announced out
69	loud. **Architectural work stops once**, after the design file is written and
70	self-reviewed, and waits for a yes. Restructuring a system on an unexamined
71	assumption is the failure that gate exists to prevent, and one pause is cheaper
72	than the rebuild.
73	
74	### Asking questions
75	
76	- One question per message. Prefer multiple choice; open-ended is fine.
77	- Aim at purpose, constraints, success criteria — not implementation trivia.
78	- Explore the repo first: files, docs, recent commits. Follow existing patterns.
79	- **YAGNI ruthlessly.** Strip speculative features out of every approach before
80	  presenting it (see `code-yoda`).
81	- **Design for isolation.** Units with one clear purpose and a well-defined
82	  interface, understandable and testable without reading their internals. A file
83	  growing large is a signal it does too much.
84	- Fix problems in existing code only where they block the work. No unrelated
85	  refactoring.
86	
87	### Showing instead of telling
88	
89	Some design questions are settled in ten seconds by a picture and never by three
90	paragraphs. **skillator has no separate mockup tool for this — the artboard gate
91	in `skillator:design-arwen` (`references/canvas.md`) is it**, and it delegates
92	the canvas itself to the `design` skill. One implementation, already carrying the
93	real palette, the real type scale and the chosen signature.
94	
95	**Offer it just-in-time, never upfront.** Wait until a question would genuinely
96	be clearer shown than described — a real layout, flow or comparison question, not
97	merely a *topic* that happens to be visual. The first time that happens, offer it
98	**as its own message**, nothing else in it, and wait:
99	
100	> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can lay the screens out on a
101	> canvas you can move things around in. Want me to?"
102	
103	Declined → continue in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.
104	
105	**Then decide per question, not once.** Accepting makes the canvas *available*;
106	it does not route every question through it. The test is: would they understand
107	this better by seeing it than by reading it?
108	
109	- **Canvas** — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, screen flows, where a
110	  signature element lands.
111	- **Terminal** — requirements, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C text
112	  options, scope decisions. "What does *personality* mean here?" is a
113	  conceptual question even though the subject is UI.
114	
115	**Their edits are decisions, not suggestions.** They save a new version of the
116	canvas; re-read the artifact before building and build from *their* version, not
117	the one you drafted. Ask only where an edit breaks a floor — a contrast failure,
118	a touch target under 44px.
119	
120	**Not a UI question?** One architecture or data-flow diagram does not want a
121	canvas: draw it inline (a mermaid block, or `artifact-diagramming` if the page
122	warrants one) and keep going.
123	
124	---
125	
126	## 2. The TASKS block is an implementation plan (`superpowers:writing-plans`)
127	
128	`TASKS:` in the design contract is not a bullet list of intentions. A build agent
129	sees **only its own task** — never the design conversation — so each task must
130	stand alone. Bounded and architectural paths both use this shape; a spike has no
131	tasks.
132	
133	### CONSTRAINTS: — what stays true across every task
134	
135	The design contract carries a `CONSTRAINTS:` field alongside `TASKS:`, and it is
136	not optional on the bounded or architectural path:
137	
138	```markdown
139	CONSTRAINTS:
140	- <exact value, name, format, or relationship every task must respect>
141	- <…>
142	```
143	
144	It holds the binding requirements that outlive any single task — exact values,
145	names, formats, and the stated relationships between components. Not per-task
146	detail: this is the part that is still true when task 6 is written by an agent
147	that never read task 1. A constraint belongs here when violating it in one task
148	silently breaks another.
149	
150	The controller reads it straight off the design file and copies it **verbatim**
151	into every task reviewer's prompt as `[GLOBAL_CONSTRAINTS]`
152	([`practice/prompts.md` §2](practice/prompts.md#2-task-reviewer)) and into the
153	implementer's brief. It is the one thing every subagent sees regardless of which
154	task it drew. A design with no cross-task invariants writes `CONSTRAINTS: none`
155	— explicitly, so the controller knows the field was considered rather than
156	forgotten.
157	
158	```markdown
159	### Task N: <component>
160	
161	**Files:**
162	- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
163	- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
164	- Test:   `tests/exact/path/test_file.py`
165	
166	**Interfaces:**
167	- Consumes: <exact signatures this task uses from earlier tasks>
168	- Produces: <exact names, parameter and return types later tasks rely on>
169	
170	- [ ] Step 1: write the failing test   <actual test code>
171	- [ ] Step 2: run it, confirm it fails <exact command + expected failure>
172	- [ ] Step 3: minimal implementation   <actual code>
173	- [ ] Step 4: run it, confirm it passes<exact command>
174	- [ ] Step 5: commit                   <exact git command>
175	```
176	
177	**Task right-sizing:** a task is the smallest unit that carries its own test
178	cycle and is worth a fresh reviewer's gate. Fold setup, config, scaffolding and
179	docs into the task whose deliverable needs them. Split only where a reviewer
180	could reject one task while approving its neighbour. Each task ends with an
181	independently testable deliverable.
182	
183	**No placeholders.** These are design failures, never write them: "TBD",
184	"implement later", "add appropriate error handling", "add validation", "write
185	tests for the above" without the test code, "similar to Task N" instead of
186	repeating the code, a step that says what without showing how, a reference to a
187	type or function no task defines.
188	
189	---
190	
191	## 3. Self-review the design before anyone builds it
192	
193	Run this yourself, inline, on the design file. Not a subagent, not a second pass.
194	
195	1. **Coverage** — walk each requirement in the request; point at the task that
196	   implements it. A requirement with no task means a missing task.
197	2. **Placeholders** — scan for every pattern in the list above. Fix them.
198	3. **Type consistency** — do the signatures, names and property spellings used in
199	   later tasks match what earlier tasks define? `clearLayers()` in Task 3 and
200	   `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug shipped in the plan.
201	4. **Contradictions and ambiguity** — could a requirement be read two ways? Pick
202	   one and make it explicit.
203	5. **Scope** — still one coherent implementation, or does it want decomposing?
204	
205	Fix inline and move on. No re-review loop.
206	
207	**A second pair of eyes — the one condition.** The five checks above are yours,
208	inline, always. They are never delegated and never re-run as a second pass; that
209	rule stands. Separately, and *after* they are done and their fixes applied, an
210	**architectural** design may be worth one independent read before anyone builds
211	from it. Dispatch [`practice/prompts.md` §5](practice/prompts.md#5-design-reviewer)
212	on a deep-tier model when **all three** hold:
213	
214	1. The path is architectural — a spike or bounded design never earns it.
215	2. The build is expensive enough that a wrong design costs more than the review:
216	   roughly six or more tasks, or any task fanning out to parallel implementers.
217	3. The design defines an interface other components will depend on, so a mistake
218	   is not local to one task.
219	
220	Its output is findings on a document, not a gate: fix what it finds, ignore what
221	you disagree with and say why, then go. It does not loop either, and it does not
222	replace the approval gate in §1 — that is the user's, not a reviewer's.
223	
224	---
225	
226	## 4. Building (`skillator:tasks-sentinels`, `test-driven-development`)
227	
228	**The iron law:** no production code without a failing test first. Wrote code
229	before the test? Delete it — don't keep it as reference, don't adapt it while
230	writing the test. Implement fresh from the test.
231	
232	The law binds behaviour, not one-liners: a config value, a doc line or a rename
233	carries no test. `code-yoda` governs which is which — non-trivial logic (a branch,
234	a loop, a parser, a money or security path) leaves one runnable check behind.
235	
236	The cycle is RED (write the failing test) → verify RED (watch it fail, for the
237	*expected* reason) → GREEN (minimal code) → verify GREEN (watch it pass, output
238	pristine) → REFACTOR. A test you never watched fail has never proven it can catch
239	anything. **[`practice/tdd.md`](practice/tdd.md)** has the cycle in full, the
240	rules that keep a test honest (name the break it catches; no mirror assertions;
241	no change detectors; assert real behavior, never mock behavior), and the
242	checklist.
243	
244	**Per task, not per build:** each build agent gets one task (build-jarvis mode
245	single: one agent, the blocks in order), fresh context, the design file path
246	and the design's `CONSTRAINTS:` — never the session history.
247	When a task comes back,
248	review it against its own spec before dispatching the next: spec compliance
249	first, then code quality. A failed review goes back to a fix agent with the
250	finding, not to the next task. Independent tasks fan out in parallel; tasks that
251	touch the same files do not.
252	
253	Use the least powerful tier that can fill each seat, and **always name the model
254	explicitly** — an omitted model inherits the session's, usually the most
255	expensive. The tiers are the four in `PLATFORMS.md`, and there are no others:
256	**cheap** for transcription and single-file mechanical work, **build** for
257	multi-file integration and for reading a task's diff, **deep** for design
258	judgement and for the final whole-branch review. The escalated fix round goes a
259	tier above the implementer that got stuck.
260	[`practice/task-loop.md` §Model selection](practice/task-loop.md#model-selection)
261	maps every seat in the loop to one of them; `PLATFORMS.md`'s Role tiers table
262	turns the tier into the slug you type on this host.
263	
264	**The controller runs a bounded loop, not an open one:** dispatch → review → at
265	most three fix rounds → adjudicate whatever is still open → one whole-branch
266	review at the end. Three is the same count as §7's three-fix rule, and for the
267	same reason. **[`practice/task-loop.md`](practice/task-loop.md)** is the
268	procedure; **[`practice/prompts.md`](practice/prompts.md)** is the text you
269	dispatch.
270	
271	### Rationalizations
272	
273	Nine of the eleven rows in
274	[`practice/tdd.md`](practice/tdd.md#common-rationalizations) — the canonical
275	table — reproduced verbatim, because this file is read every session and tdd.md
276	is not. The two not here ("I need to explore first", "Existing code here has no
277	tests") are in tdd.md.
278	
279	| Excuse | Reality |
280	|---|---|
281	| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. The test takes thirty seconds. |
282	| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately, which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. |
283	| "Spirit not ritual — tests after are the same" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code already in front of you: you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you would have discovered. |
284	| "I already tested it manually" | No record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" is not comprehensive. |
285	| "Deleting hours of work is wasteful" | Sunk cost. That time is spent either way. Keeping code you cannot trust is the waste. |
286	| "Keep it as reference, tests first from now" | You will adapt it. That is testing after. Delete means delete. |
287	| "This is hard to test" | Listen to the test. Hard to test is hard to use — it is telling you about the design. |
288	| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD *is* the pragmatic path: bugs caught before commit, regressions prevented, refactoring without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production. |
289	| "Just this once" | No. |
290	
291	**Red flags — each means delete the code and start over:** code before test ·
292	test passes immediately · you cannot explain why the test failed · "tests added
293	later" · "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic" · "this is different because…"
294	
295	---
296	
297	## 5. Claiming it works (`verification-before-completion`)
298	
299	```
300	NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
301	```
302	
303	Before writing "done", "fixed", "passing", or the Outcome section:
304	
305	1. **Identify** the command that proves the claim.
306	2. **Run** it, in full, now — not from memory of an earlier run.
307	3. **Read** the whole output: exit code, failure count.
308	4. **Verify** the output actually confirms the claim.
309	5. **Then** claim it, with the evidence attached.
310	
311	Skipping a step is not verifying. A test suite that was green three edits ago is
312	not evidence. If it fails, say so with the output and feed it to rework.
313	
314	| Claim | Requires | Not sufficient |
315	|---|---|---|
316	| Tests pass | Test output, 0 failures | A previous run, "should pass" |
317	| Linter clean | Linter output, 0 errors | A partial check, extrapolation |
318	| Build succeeds | Build command, exit 0 | Linter passing, logs looking fine |
319	| Bug fixed | The original symptom retested, passing | Code changed, assumed fixed |
320	| Regression test works | Red-green verified: revert the fix, watch it fail, restore | It passed once |
321	| Agent completed | The diff shows the changes | The agent reported success |
322	| Requirements met | Line-by-line against the design | Tests passing |
323	
324	**Red flags — stop:** "should", "probably", "seems to" · "Great!" / "Perfect!" /
325	"Done!" before running anything · about to commit or push without verifying ·
326	trusting an agent's success report · partial verification · "just this once" ·
327	being tired and wanting it over · **any wording implying success you have not
328	run**.
329	
330	| Excuse | Reality |
331	|---|---|
332	| "Should work now" | Run it. |
333	| "I'm confident" | Confidence is not evidence. |
334	| "The linter passed" | The linter is not the compiler. |
335	| "The agent said success" | Verify independently — check the diff. |
336	| "A partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing. |
337	| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion is not an exemption. |
338	| "Different words, so the rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter. |
339	
340	---
341	
342	## 6. Reviewing, and taking review
343	
344	**Requesting it.** At the end of a build, before wrap-up: dispatch one reviewer
345	over the whole diff with crafted context — the design file and the diff by path,
346	never the session history — on the **deep** tier, never the session default.
347	[`practice/prompts.md` §4](practice/prompts.md#4-final-reviewer) is the template.
348	`code-review:code-review` and `skillator:audit-sherlock` are the packaged
349	alternatives on a large surface. Findings feed rework and the Outcome section
350	gets updated, so the record stays true.
351	
352	**Receiving it** — from a human, a reviewer agent, or a PR comment. Review is a
353	technical claim to evaluate, not a social event:
354	
355	1. **Read** the whole thing before reacting.
356	2. **Understand** — restate the requirement in your own words, or ask.
357	3. **Verify** it against this codebase. Correct-in-general can be wrong here.
358	4. **Evaluate** — is it technically sound *for this code*?
359	5. **Respond** — a technical acknowledgement, or reasoned pushback.
360	6. **Implement** one item at a time, testing each.
361	
362	Never "You're absolutely right!", "Great point!", or "Let me implement that now"
363	before step 3. Restate, ask, push back with reasoning, or just start working.
364	
365	**Unclear on any item? Stop and ask before implementing any of them.** Items are
366	usually related; partial understanding produces the wrong change to the ones you
367	did understand.
368	
369	---
370	
371	## 7. Debugging
372	
373	```
374	NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
375	```
376	
377	Symptom fixes are failure. When the task is a bug this runs **before** the design
378	— what it finds is the input the design needs. It applies to any technical issue:
379	test failure, production bug, wrong output, performance, build, integration.
380	Especially under time pressure, and especially when a fix seems obvious.
381	
382	**Phase 1 — root cause.** Read the error and the whole stack trace; they often
383	contain the answer. Reproduce consistently — if you can't, gather more data
384	rather than guess. Check what changed: `git diff`, recent commits, new deps,
385	config, environment. In a multi-component system, instrument each boundary — log
386	what enters and what leaves — run it once, and let the evidence say *which*
387	component fails before you look inside one. Trace a bad value backwards to where
388	it originates and fix it there, not where it surfaced —
389	[`practice/debugging.md`](practice/debugging.md) has the tracing procedure, plus
390	defense-in-depth for after the fix, condition-based waiting for flaky tests, and
391	the bisect for a test that only fails inside the suite.
392	
393	**Phase 2 — pattern.** Find working code that is similar, in this same codebase.
394	Read the reference implementation completely, not skimmed. List every difference
395	between working and broken, however small — "that can't matter" is where the bug
396	lives. Check dependencies, config, and the assumptions the working one makes.
397	
398	**Phase 3 — hypothesis.** State one: "I think X is the root cause because Y."
399	Test it with the smallest possible change, one variable at a time. It worked →
400	Phase 4. It didn't → form a *new* hypothesis; never stack another fix on top.
401	Don't understand something? Say so.
402	
403	**Phase 4 — fix.** Write the failing test case first (§4's law applies). Make one
404	change addressing the root cause — no "while I'm here" improvements, no bundled
405	refactor. Verify through §5's gate: the test passes, nothing else broke, the
406	issue is actually gone.
407	
408	**The three-fix rule.** Fix didn't work? Count the attempts. Under three: back to
409	Phase 1 with the new information. **At three: stop and question the
410	architecture** — each fix revealing a new problem somewhere else, or demanding
411	"massive refactoring", is not a failed hypothesis, it is a wrong design. There is
412	no fourth attempt at the same defect.
413	
414	This is the **same rule and the same count** as the task loop's fix rounds. In a
415	debugging session you raise it with the user; inside the task loop the controller
416	adjudicates first and asks the user only when every path forward is a guess
417	([`practice/task-loop.md` §4](practice/task-loop.md#4-the-fix-loop--three-rounds-then-a-breaker)
418	is the procedure). Three attempts, then stop fixing and question the design —
419	that part does not vary by context.
420	
421	**Red flags — every one of these means return to Phase 1:** "quick fix now,
422	investigate later" · "just try X and see" · several changes at once, then run
423	tests · "skip the test, I'll check by hand" · "it's probably X" · listing fixes
424	before tracing data flow · "one more attempt" at attempt three · "the loop allows
425	me another round" — it does not, the count is three there too.
426	
427	---
428	
429	## 8. Branch lifecycle
430	
431	**Isolation, before parallel work.** Check whether you are *already* isolated
432	first: `git rev-parse --git-dir` differing from `--git-common-dir` means a linked
433	worktree — don't create a second one. That test is also true inside a submodule,
434	so rule that out with `git rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree`. In a
435	normal checkout, ask consent before creating a worktree unless the user has
436	already stated a preference; honor a stated preference without asking.
437	
438	Prefer the **host's native worktree tool** (`EnterWorktree`, a `/worktree`
439	command, a `--worktree` flag) over `git worktree add` — a manual worktree creates
440	state the harness can neither see nor clean up. Fall back to git only where there
441	is no native tool. Parallel build agents that would touch the same files need
442	this; agents on disjoint files do not.
443	
444	Falling back to git, pick the directory in this order — an explicit user
445	preference always beats observed state: (1) a worktree directory the user has
446	already named; (2) an existing project-local worktree directory, if the repo
447	already has one — follow the convention that is there; (3) a sibling of the repo
448	root, `../<repo>-worktrees/<branch>`, never nested inside the repo where it will
449	be picked up by globs, watchers and test runners. Then run the project's setup —
450	install, env file, build — because a fresh worktree has none of it.
451	
452	**Finishing.** Run the project's full suite first — a failing suite means report
453	the failures and stop, not offer a menu. Then detect the environment (normal repo
454	/ named-branch worktree / detached HEAD), confirm which base branch this work
455	forked from before merging anywhere, and present the choice rather than picking:
456	
457	```
458	1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
459	2. Push and create a Pull Request
460	3. Keep the branch as-is
461	```
462	
463	Detached HEAD drops option 1 and the workspace stays put — it is externally
464	managed. Clean up a worktree only if this session created it. Push and merge stay
465	user-confirmed on every host; `skillator:mergeprep-oracle` and `skillator:merge-smith`
466	own the conflict work.
467	
468	---
469	
470	---
471	
472	## What is not here
473	
474	This file owns process. It does not duplicate the skills that own a *surface*,
475	and `grayskull-power` still routes to those:
476	
477	| Skill | Owns |
478	|---|---|
479	| `skillator:design-arwen` | The UI/UX design itself — run it **as** the design phase when the deliverable is an interface, and its `references/canvas.md` is §1's visual companion |
480	| `skillator:live-friday` | The app running before the first edit |
481	| `skillator:audit-sherlock` | A whole-codebase forensic audit |
482	| `skillator:tickets-zordon` | `TICKETS.md`, the board |
483	| `skillator:mergeprep-oracle` / `merge-smith` | Conflicts and merge execution |
484	| `skillator:handoff-cortana` / `watch-cortana` | Continuity across context loss |
485	| `skillator:skill-smith` | Authoring or fixing a skill — `writing-skills` merged in: the description rules, form-to-failure, bulletproofing, and subagent testing |
486	
487	`dataviz` and `claude-api` are read-before-you-write references, not processes:
488	load them inside the design phase, never in front of it.
489	
490	**Provenance.** §§1-8 plus `practice/` are merged from the superpowers process
491	skills named in the table at the top, rewritten in skillator's own words so these
492	skills stand alone on hosts where superpowers isn't installed. This is a merge,
493	not a live link — if superpowers evolves, this is what needs updating.
494	
495	Three deliberate divergences from the originals:
496	
497	1. **The approval gate** in §1 — spike and bounded stay autonomous.
498	2. **The subagent prompts** in `practice/prompts.md` are host-neutral rather than
499	   written against one harness's dispatch syntax; `PLATFORMS.md` maps the
500	   dispatch mechanism and the model tiers per host.
501	3. **The visual companion** is not reimplemented. brainstorming ships its own
502	   browser mockup server; skillator routes that role to `design-arwen`'s artboard
503	   gate, which already draws in the run's real palette and type scale and reads
504	   the user's edits back as decisions.
505
